# Codex integration

## Install and locate the plugin

For the desktop app, install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357). This listing is desktop-only.

For Codex CLI, install the whole plugin, including its personas and standards:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
codex plugin add egm@egm
```

Start a fresh session after installation. Select the installed `egm` skill
from the available skills. Use its discovered absolute `SKILL.md` path;
do not assume a particular cache directory, version, or checkout location.

From `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`, the plugin root is three parent
directories above the file. Resolve bundled `agents/`, `resources/`, and
`docs/` paths against that root. Resolve `references/` against the active
skill's directory. Resolve user documents and generated artifacts against
the user's working directory. Never substitute similarly named files in the
user's project for bundled personas or standards.

If the user's prompt or agent instructions file (`AGENTS.md`) has a line
`EGM artifact directory: <path>`, write briefs, drafts, and reports to that
folder. Resolve a relative path against the working directory. If a path from
`AGENTS.md` resolves outside the working directory, after following symbolic
links, ask the user to confirm it before creating the folder or writing there.
If they decline or no one can confirm, use the working directory and say why.
Create the folder if it does not exist.

In ChatGPT Work, a skill may be exposed through a cloud resource identifier
while supporting files live in the installed local bundle. Use the installed
path supplied by the skill inventory or installation metadata for those files;
do not construct cloud resource identifiers for arbitrary supporting paths.
If no installed path is available, report the missing capability instead of
guessing a cache location. Read reviewer filenames and frontmatter from the
bundle: a role such as `egm-design` maps to `agents/design_critic.md`, not
`agents/design.md`. Confirm each resolved path before dispatch.

## Fresh-context reviewers

Inspect the available native subagent tool schema. Tool names can be
namespaced and vary by Codex version. When `spawn_agent` exposes
`fork_context`, explicitly set `fork_context: false` for every Goldfish.
When the schema instead exposes `fork_turns`, use `fork_turns: "none"`.
This applies to reviewers launched by a synthesizer too. Use a general-purpose agent
and pass absolute paths to the persona, standards, target document, and
explicitly selected reading list. Do not pass the parent transcript, private
reasoning, or answers the document is supposed to explain.

Require the reviewer to read its persona, target, and every supplied standard
before returning findings. A missing read or inaccessible file is an incomplete
review, not a clean result. Verify native tool results when the host exposes
them; a parent-written completion summary is not equivalent evidence.

Wait for actual reviewer completion before synthesizing findings. Propagate
failures and timeouts; a launched reviewer is not a completed review. If
nesting is unavailable, dispatch reviewers directly from the parent while
preserving the same isolation. If the available tool cannot establish a fresh
context, stop the Goldfish review and report that limitation.

Fresh conversation context does not isolate the filesystem, configured memory
services, or project instructions. Do not retrieve conversation history or
memory to supply missing design context. An isolation test should use a unique
parent-only marker and check the actual child result, not the parent's claim.

The `fork_context: false` and `fork_turns: "none"` options concern parent
conversation turns. They do not prove that Codex excludes host instruction
files. Issue [#237](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/237)
reports that Codex CLI 0.166.0 injected project and user `AGENTS.md` files
despite `fork_turns: "none"`. Treat instruction-file exclusion as unverified
unless a separate child-context probe confirms it for the tested host version.

## Questions and artifacts

The shared skills' question payloads describe the intended interaction, not a
literal Codex API. Use a structured question tool only when it is available
and permitted in the current mode, mapping to its actual schema. Otherwise
ask one plain-text question and wait for the answer. Preserve the skill's
readiness and section approval gates; tool unavailability is not approval.

Link generated artifacts with absolute-path Markdown links such as
`[design draft](/absolute/project/design_draft.md)`. For paths containing
spaces use `[design draft](</absolute/my project/design_draft.md>)`.
Do not use `file://` links in Codex chat.

## Verification

Run the offline packaging checks with `pytest tests/unit`. The opt-in native
workflow tests are documented in [TESTING.md](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/TESTING.md). They require
an authenticated Codex CLI and consume model usage. Installing or discovering
the plugin alone does not establish end-to-end workflow support.

## ChatGPT

Install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357) in the ChatGPT desktop app. This listing is desktop-only; it does not establish support for cloud Work sessions.

### Test a local package

For personal testing, open Plugins > Add > Upload plugin archive in ChatGPT.
Package the runtime files from the repository root:

```sh
python3 scripts/pack_plugin.py --target openai --output /tmp/egm-chatgpt
```

Use a fresh output directory. Upload `/tmp/egm-chatgpt/egm-openai.zip` and
install the plugin in the ChatGPT desktop app. Use
**Try in chat** in a new thread that runs locally. The earlier cloud Work
test in `TESTING.md` predates this package's desktop-only declaration.
Keep repository marketplace catalogs and development files outside this archive.
The OpenAI directory package declares local execution because bootstrap uses
shell commands. Its listing uses the portable manifest's OpenAI extension;
the Codex compatibility manifest retains matching metadata for native installs.
Keep `.claude-plugin/` outside the OpenAI archive: its agent adapters belong
to the Claude Code integration. Public directory plugins cannot include hooks.

Enterprise, Business, and Edu workspaces can import the plugin via Admin > Plugins > Add > Import marketplace.
Set the repository URL to `https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model` and marketplace path to `.agents/plugins`.
Skills are accessible via `@egm` for direct interaction.
Check the native tools in the current chat before starting a Goldfish review.
Some ChatGPT Work sessions expose native `spawn_agent` with `fork_turns: "none"`.
Use the fresh-context instructions above when those tools are available. If
they are absent, stop and report that isolation is unavailable; never simulate
reviewers in the parent context. Availability in one Work session does not
establish support across every ChatGPT mode or account.
# Execution Instructions

This file holds bundled execution rules shared across multiple Elephant-Goldfish
Model (EGM) skills, plus drafting-only rules used strictly by `egm-draft`. Only
apply the sections referenced by the active skill.

## Plugin-Root Resource Paths

Bundled personas (`agents/<file>.md`), standards
(`resources/document_standards/<name>.md`), harness guides (`docs/*.md`), and
this file (`resources/execution_instructions.md`) sit at the plugin root, two
directories above each skill's folder (`<plugin-root>/skills/<skill-name>/`).

*   **Local / relative path**: Read `../../resources/execution_instructions.md`
    (or `<plugin-root>/<path>`).
*   **Claude Code and Cowork**: Read
    `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/resources/execution_instructions.md` (or
    `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/<path>`).
*   **Pathless `<SKILL>` injection**: If the harness injects a skill without its
    file path, check `~/.gemini/config/plugins/egm/<path>`.

Pass spawned subagents the resolved absolute paths of their persona file and
standard when `<plugin-root>` is known. A failed skill-relative lookup does not
mean the file is absent from the plugin.
Never substitute workspace files with similar names for bundled personas,
standards, or execution instructions. If you cannot read a required plugin-root
file after resolving `<plugin-root>`, say so instead of calling it missing; apply
the active skill's inline fallback only when file tools are unavailable.

## Subagent Delegation (Goldfish Isolation)

Applies to subagent-spawning skills (`egm-bootstrap`, `egm-brainstorm`,
`egm-review`, and `egm-review-loop`):

A Goldfish runs in a fresh context with no conversation history. Spawn each
subagent with your harness's subagent tool (Antigravity: `invoke_subagent`;
Claude Code: `Agent`; Codex: `spawn_agent`). Each subagent is defined in
`agents/<file>.md`, and its frontmatter `name` (for example `egm-zoom-out`) is
the subagent type to request where your harness registers named subagents.
Otherwise spawn a general-purpose subagent and tell it to read that persona
file first. Pass prompts verbatim and wait for the report. If your harness
cannot nest subagents, use direct dispatch instead of `egm-synthesizer` (see
[harnesses.md](../docs/harnesses.md)). If your harness has no subagent tool,
follow the active skill's fallback rule (`egm-bootstrap` runs scout steps
inline; `egm-review`, `egm-brainstorm`, and `egm-review-loop` stop and tell the
user that a review in the same context is not a Goldfish review).

## Shared Design & Review Constraints

Applies strictly to `egm-brainstorm`, `egm-draft`, and `egm-review` (not
`egm-bootstrap`):

*   **Artifact-First Delivery (MANDATORY)**: You are **STRICTLY FORBIDDEN** from
    presenting large proposals, drafts, summaries, or review reports directly in
    the chat pane. Write them directly to the working directory (or your
    harness's artifact directory, if one is configured) via your file-writing
    tool, share the file path or clickable link in chat, and ask the user for
    review.
*   **Plain-English Standard**: Write concepts briefs, specs, summaries,
    reports, and communications in simple, direct, jargon-free plain English.
    Explain technical mechanisms concretely. Do not summarize away substance or
    rely on buzzwords, promotional adjectives (*seamless*, *robust*,
    *blazingly fast*), or decorative adverbs (*seamlessly*, *effortlessly*,
    *literally*, *drastically*, *obviously*).
*   **Adversarial Rigor (No Sycophancy)**: Never agree by default. Stress-test
    ideas, strategies, and opinions to find weak points, edge cases, and blind
    spots before affirming anything. Lead with what is wrong, missing, or risky
    before highlighting merits. Never parrot user framing or validate asserted
    conclusions reflexively; surface what the user is missing, the strongest
    counter-argument, and whether the opposing view holds. Only agree after
    rigorous, objective scrutiny.
    *   **Banned Adjectives (No Flattery)**: Never use validating adjectives
        like `"brilliant"`, `"great"`, `"smart"`, `"correct"`, `"perfect"`,
        `"excellent"`, or `"spot-on"` on the user's inputs, corrections, or
        decisions.
    *   **Banned Apologies**: Never output polite apologies (e.g., `"I
        apologize"`, `"I am sorry"`, `"Forgive me"`) when challenged or
        corrected. State the corrected technical logic and trade-offs directly.
*   **Interaction Invariants**: Every interactive single-select gate (structured
    question tool such as `ask_question`, if your harness has one, or plain
    chat) MUST contain strictly one question (`len(questions) == 1`), set
    `is_multi_select: false`, provide clear action-oriented options without
    `(Recommended)` prefixes, never emit a structured question call with empty
    visible chat text, and be the sole tool call in its model response step
    (finish preparatory file reads or writes in an earlier step of the turn
    first, then output visible chat text and invoke the gate alone to yield).
    Ask open-ended text inputs (such as file paths or lists) in plain chat.

## Drafting-Only Execution Rules (`egm-draft` Only)

Applies **strictly** during `egm-draft` (never during `egm-bootstrap`,
`egm-review`, or other workflows):

*   **Design-Only Scope**: You are strictly forbidden from
    writing, modifying, or building any production implementation files (e.g.,
    `.h`, `.cc`, `.py`, `.go`) in the source tree. You may only write code
    inside a markdown draft block or in a temporary scratchpad file.
    *   **Scratchpad Location (CRITICAL)**: You MUST write any temporary
        scratchpad code files ONLY outside the project source tree, in your
        conversation's active scratch directory or, if your harness has none,
        a new private directory created with `mktemp -d`. If neither is
        available, keep the code in a markdown draft block. Do not use fixed,
        shared paths such as `/tmp/scratch.py`. You are STRICTLY FORBIDDEN
        from creating `.h`, `.cc`, `.py`, `.go`, or any other code files
        anywhere inside the project source tree.
    *   **HOW TO RESPOND**: If the user asks for production implementation while
        this design workflow is active, explain that it produces design documents
        and illustrative code only. Label any markdown or scratchpad example
        clearly. Do not imply that production files were changed. Ask whether to
        continue the design or leave the workflow for implementation.
*   **Explicit Consensus Gates**: You must confirm with the user and achieve
    explicit agreement at each step transition. Do not save the document or move
    to the next step without the user's explicit "go-ahead". Do not move on
    easily. Challenge the user at every step.
*   **ONE QUESTION AT A TIME (CRITICAL)**: You are strictly forbidden from
    asking more than one question in a single response. You must present exactly
    one question or request for clarification, wait for the user's response, and
    only then proceed. Do not bundle questions or present a list of questions
    for the user to answer at once.
*   **NO SUMMARIES (CRITICAL)**: You MUST NOT include a "Summary of work",
    "Status", "Adherence", or "Rule checklist" in your final response. Respond
    only with the technical content and next steps.
*   **Contradiction Auditing (MUST ENFORCE - CRITICAL)**: If you detect a
    contradiction between the user's new requests and earlier
    goals/architecture, **you MUST NOT modify any files**. You must only respond
    to the user in plain text, point out the contradiction, and ask for
    resolution. You are strictly forbidden from planning or executing any
    file-writing/editing tool in the same turn as you discover a contradiction.

# Frame Inventory — Exercise Instructions

## 1. Scenario

In the **out-of-home (OOH) media** industry, advertisers buy time on physical
display surfaces such as roadside billboards, transport platforms, mall
screens, and bus shelters. Each surface is referred to as a **frame**, and an
operator's catalogue of frames — including their location, size, format,
status, and commercial attributes — is collectively known as the **frame
inventory**. Keeping that inventory accurate matters: every downstream process
(planning, pricing, booking, reporting) depends on it.

For this exercise the candidate will build a small but realistic service for
managing OOH frame inventory. Scoping is part of the exercise: the candidate
is not expected to deliver every feature one could imagine, but to pick a
meaningful subset and deliver it well.

## 2. What we provide

This repository is the starting point. It is intentionally minimal so the
candidate can make their own architectural choices, but it includes enough
infrastructure to skip the boilerplate and start delivering business value
straight away.

| Path                  | Contents                                                                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/backend/`        | Bare Spring Boot 3.5 + Java 21 module (Gradle). Exposes only `/api/health`.       |
| `src/frontend/`       | Next.js + React 19 + TypeScript module that calls the backend `/api/health` on boot. |
| `docker-compose.yml`  | One-command infra: backend, frontend, MongoDB, Postgres, OpenSearch + Dashboards.  |
| `data/`               | Extract from the legacy system — `inventory_frame.csv` (~1.3k OOH frame rows).    |
| `design-system/`      | Design system the frontend must be built against — components, tokens, guidance.  |
| `README.md`           | How to run the stack locally, ports, and credentials for the bundled services.    |

> **A note on the suggested infrastructure.** The `docker-compose.yml` file
> is a starting point, not a requirement. The candidate is free to swap any
> of these services for tooling they prefer (a different database, search
> engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final stack
> still runs end-to-end with a single command. If the candidate does choose
> to use the services provided here, they should pick **one** of the two
> datastores for their domain data — either `mongodb` *or* `postgres`,
> not both — and remove the service they don't need (along with its volume)
> so the stack reflects the design actually built.

In addition, the candidate receives:

- A **provisioned OpenAI Codex API key**. Use of an AI coding assistant is
  explicitly expected — we want to see how the candidate collaborates with a
  model, not whether they can hand-write every line.

## 3. Features

The candidate should deliver the following features:

1. **Add a frame.** A user can create a new frame through the application and
   see it persisted in the inventory.
2. **Edit a frame.** A user can amend an existing frame's attributes and have
   the changes saved.
3. **Bulk upload frames from a CSV.** A user can upload a CSV through the
   application and have the rows ingested into the inventory. The supplied
   `data/inventory_frame.csv` is the file to validate this feature
   against. This is a user-driven feature of the running app, not a one-off
   bootstrap step.
4. **View a frame's history.** A user can see the audit trail of changes to
   any given frame.

How these features are surfaced, structured, and tested is left to the
candidate's judgement.

## 4. Domain data

The shape of a frame is anchored by the legacy export shipped at
`data/inventory_frame.csv` (~1,300 rows) and by the prototype in
`design-system/`. The candidate is expected to inspect both and design a
domain model they are comfortable defending.

At a high level, each frame in the export carries:

- **Identity** — a frame identifier, plus references to downstream systems
  (Broadsign, pricing, linked frames).
- **Location** — country, region, town, postcode, latitude/longitude,
  address, and distance to the nearest school.
- **Site & position** — the kind of place the frame lives in (station,
  underground, roadside, airport, etc.) and where on that site it sits.
- **Format** — classic vs digital, format code, dimensions / pixels /
  aspect ratio, illumination, number of slots, size grouping.
- **Lifecycle** — created/modified timestamps, status, and a status reason.
- **Commercials** — impact weight, pricing grade, production rate card,
  premium flag.

The legacy column names and groupings are not prescriptive — the candidate
should design the domain model that best fits the features in §3, and
document the assumptions they made along the way.

## 5. Additional Requirements

Install and use the **[Entire CLI](https://entire.io)**. Entire hooks into the
candidate's git workflow and, on every push, captures the Codex agent
sessions that produced the changes and links them to the corresponding
commits as *checkpoints*. The result is a searchable record of how the
solution was actually built: the prompts used, the iterations the candidate
went through, the suggestions they accepted, and — just as important — the
ones they rejected or refined.

This is not about surveillance; it is about giving us a fair signal of
**how** the candidate works with AI tooling. We are far less interested in
whether code came from a human keystroke or a model completion than in
whether the candidate exercised judgement, scoped well, and reviewed the
output critically.

> **Note:** Codex support in Entire is currently in preview. The candidate
> should follow Entire's setup documentation for the latest supported
> workflow.

## 6. Submission

When the candidate is ready, they should share a **public GitHub repository**
containing their solution. The repository must include:

- All source code and anything else required to run the solution.
- A README explaining how to run it, the design decisions taken, and the
  trade-offs made.
- The Entire **checkpoints branch** with the captured Codex sessions linked
  to commits, so we can review the AI collaboration alongside the code.

There is no fixed deadline; we recommend timeboxing the exercise to a few
focused sessions rather than open-ended work. If something blocks progress,
note it in the README rather than over-investing time on it.
# AGENTS.md - Java Spring Boot & gRPC Development Guidelines

Behavioral and architectural guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes while strictly enforcing **SOLID principles**, Spring Boot + gRPC best practices, and clean code standards.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:

* State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
* If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently.
* If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
* If something is unclear (e.g., `.proto` contract changes, transaction boundaries, or domain invariants), stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

* No features or RPC endpoints beyond what was asked.
* No abstractions or Strategy interfaces for single-use code (apply OCP when variation actually exists or is requested).
* No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
* No defensive `try-catch` blocks or error handling for impossible scenarios.
* If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
* Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
* If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it — don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

* Remove imports, variables, fields, or private methods that YOUR changes made unused.
* Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
* "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
* "Refactor X" → "Ensure unit and gRPC integration tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]
[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

## 5. Tech Stack & Conventions

* **Language:** Java 21+ (Prefer `record` for immutable domain DTOs/commands, pattern matching, and modern standard library features).
* **Framework:** Spring Boot 3.4+ with **Spring gRPC** (`org.springframework.grpc:spring-grpc-spring-boot-starter`).
* **Serialization / RPC:** Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) & gRPC.
* **Build Tool:** Maven or Gradle (Respect existing project configuration and `protobuf` compiler plugins).
* **Dependency Injection:** **ALWAYS** use Constructor Injection. Field injection (`@Autowired` on fields) is strictly forbidden.
* **Null Safety:** Avoid returning `null` from methods. Use `Optional<T>` for repository/service lookups that may not yield a result, and use `@NonNull` / `@Nullable` annotations where appropriate.

## 6. Build, Protobuf & Test Commands

Use these standard commands to compile Protobuf definitions and verify changes:

* **Maven:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./mvnw protobuf:compile protobuf:compile-custom`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./mvnw test`
  * Run a single test class: `./mvnw test -Dtest=ClassName`
* **Gradle:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./gradlew generateProto`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./gradlew test`
  * Run a single test class: `./gradlew test --tests "*ClassName"`

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

# Frame Inventory Design System

A focused product design system extracted from the **Frame Inventory** prototype (an OOH out-of-home media operations tool). Built on top of the Global Design System (Global Next theme — Inter type, blue/cyan palette) and extended with the patterns this product introduced: inventory tables, master-data drawers, audit timelines, and stepper-driven creation flows.

## Sources
- `tokens.css` — full Global Design System tokens (Inter font, color palettes, semantic roles, spacing, elevation).
- `styles.css` — component styles built on top of the tokens (buttons, chips, tables, fields, surfaces, banners, timeline).
- `shell.jsx` — app chrome: rail nav, topbar, breadcrumbs, brand mark, icon set.
- `master-data.jsx`, `direction-a.jsx`, `direction-b.jsx` — production-shape examples consumed by the design system.

## Index
- `tokens.css` — design tokens (variables only — copy/import directly).
- `styles.css` — component styles built on those tokens.
- `preview/` — design-system preview cards (rendered in the Design System tab).
- `SKILL.md` — Agent Skill manifest for downstream prompting.
- `Frame Inventory.html` — the prototype that anchors the system.

## Content fundamentals
- **Tone**: operational, factual, second-person where action is required ("Add a frame", "Pick from master data"). Never marketing-y, never exclamatory.
- **Casing**: sentence case for everything — buttons (`New frame`, not `New Frame`), headers, table columns. Acronyms keep their caps (`OOH`, `CMS`, `DSP`).
- **Copy density**: short labels, longer help text below in `--text-secondary`. Inline microcopy preferred over modals.
- **No emoji** in product surfaces. Status uses iconographic dots/chips.
- **Numbers** are factual and contextual ("412 m", "10s · 6/min", "FRM-00214"). Use middle-dot `·` as a soft separator.

## Visual foundations
- **Type**: Inter, 13px body default — dense product UI, not document-style. Headings use the same family with weight (500–600) instead of size jumps.
- **Color**: cool blue primary (`--blue-1000` #046AC4) on near-white surfaces (`--gray-50`). Neutrals do the heavy lifting — color is reserved for status (green/red/orange) and primary actions.
- **Surfaces**: white cards on a `--gray-50` canvas, separated by 1px `--border-subtle` borders. **No drop shadows** on resting surfaces — elevation is reserved for popovers and drawers (`--elev-medium`).
- **Radii**: 4px (`--radius`) for inputs/buttons, 8px (`--radius-lg`) for surfaces, 999px for chips/pills.
- **Spacing**: 8px base — `--sp-1` through `--sp-10`. Most gaps are 16–24px (`--sp-2`, `--sp-3`).
- **Hover**: subtle background tint (`--gray-50` → `--blue-50`), no scale.
- **Press**: darker shade of the same token, no scale.
- **Borders**: 1px solid `--border-subtle` for surfaces, `--border-default` for inputs.
- **Animation**: practically none — drawers slide in 160ms, banners fade 120ms. Product is utilitarian; movement is reserved for state changes.
- **Imagery**: none in the chrome. The product is text- and data-first.
- **Iconography**: hand-rolled stroke icons at 1.8px stroke (Lucide-style), defined inline in `shell.jsx`. Domain glyphs (Station / Roadside / Airport / Mall / Bus Shelter) live alongside the UI icon set.

## Iconography
Inline SVG icons exported from `shell.jsx::Icon`. Stroke weight 1.8px, round caps/joins, single-color (`currentColor`). Domain icons are 16–24px. The system covers ~30 glyphs: `search`, `plus`, `pencil`, `trash`, `chev`, `chevL`, `filter`, `map`, `list`, `pin`, `history`, `more`, `link`, `warn`, `info`, `check`, `x`, `station`, `road`, `airport`, `mall`, `bus`, `frame`, `dash`, `cog`, `report`, `school`, `globe`, `download`, `upload`.

No emoji, no third-party icon CDN. If new icons are needed, draw new SVGs in the same stroke style.

## Caveats
- The system is **product-scoped** to Frame Inventory — not yet a brand-wide system.
- No marketing surfaces (landing pages, emails) are covered.
- Dark mode is not addressed.

# Codex integration

## Install and locate the plugin

For the desktop app, install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357). This listing is desktop-only.

For Codex CLI, install the whole plugin, including its personas and standards:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
codex plugin add egm@egm
```

Start a fresh session after installation. Select the installed `egm` skill
from the available skills. Use its discovered absolute `SKILL.md` path;
do not assume a particular cache directory, version, or checkout location.

From `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`, the plugin root is three parent
directories above the file. Resolve bundled `agents/`, `resources/`, and
`docs/` paths against that root. Resolve `references/` against the active
skill's directory. Resolve user documents and generated artifacts against
the user's working directory. Never substitute similarly named files in the
user's project for bundled personas or standards.

If the user's prompt or agent instructions file (`AGENTS.md`) has a line
`EGM artifact directory: <path>`, write briefs, drafts, and reports to that
folder. Resolve a relative path against the working directory. If a path from
`AGENTS.md` resolves outside the working directory, after following symbolic
links, ask the user to confirm it before creating the folder or writing there.
If they decline or no one can confirm, use the working directory and say why.
Create the folder if it does not exist.

In ChatGPT Work, a skill may be exposed through a cloud resource identifier
while supporting files live in the installed local bundle. Use the installed
path supplied by the skill inventory or installation metadata for those files;
do not construct cloud resource identifiers for arbitrary supporting paths.
If no installed path is available, report the missing capability instead of
guessing a cache location. Read reviewer filenames and frontmatter from the
bundle: a role such as `egm-design` maps to `agents/design_critic.md`, not
`agents/design.md`. Confirm each resolved path before dispatch.

## Fresh-context reviewers

Inspect the available native subagent tool schema. Tool names can be
namespaced and vary by Codex version. When `spawn_agent` exposes
`fork_context`, explicitly set `fork_context: false` for every Goldfish.
When the schema instead exposes `fork_turns`, use `fork_turns: "none"`.
This applies to reviewers launched by a synthesizer too. Use a general-purpose agent
and pass absolute paths to the persona, standards, target document, and
explicitly selected reading list. Do not pass the parent transcript, private
reasoning, or answers the document is supposed to explain.

Require the reviewer to read its persona, target, and every supplied standard
before returning findings. A missing read or inaccessible file is an incomplete
review, not a clean result. Verify native tool results when the host exposes
them; a parent-written completion summary is not equivalent evidence.

Wait for actual reviewer completion before synthesizing findings. Propagate
failures and timeouts; a launched reviewer is not a completed review. If
nesting is unavailable, dispatch reviewers directly from the parent while
preserving the same isolation. If the available tool cannot establish a fresh
context, stop the Goldfish review and report that limitation.

Fresh conversation context does not isolate the filesystem, configured memory
services, or project instructions. Do not retrieve conversation history or
memory to supply missing design context. An isolation test should use a unique
parent-only marker and check the actual child result, not the parent's claim.

The `fork_context: false` and `fork_turns: "none"` options concern parent
conversation turns. They do not prove that Codex excludes host instruction
files. Issue [#237](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/237)
reports that Codex CLI 0.166.0 injected project and user `AGENTS.md` files
despite `fork_turns: "none"`. Treat instruction-file exclusion as unverified
unless a separate child-context probe confirms it for the tested host version.

## Questions and artifacts

The shared skills' question payloads describe the intended interaction, not a
literal Codex API. Use a structured question tool only when it is available
and permitted in the current mode, mapping to its actual schema. Otherwise
ask one plain-text question and wait for the answer. Preserve the skill's
readiness and section approval gates; tool unavailability is not approval.

Link generated artifacts with absolute-path Markdown links such as
`[design draft](/absolute/project/design_draft.md)`. For paths containing
spaces use `[design draft](</absolute/my project/design_draft.md>)`.
Do not use `file://` links in Codex chat.

workflow tests are documented in [TESTING.md](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/TESTING.md). They require
an authenticated Codex CLI and consume model usage. Installing or discovering
the plugin alone does not establish end-to-end workflow support.

The site identifiers need more care. The same `inventory_site_no` can have different postcodes and environments, and the same `site_no` can appear under different inventory sites. The EGM brainstorm skill requires clarification before the schema review and migration. The key decision is how to identify an existing frame when a CSV is uploaded again.

What should happen when a later upload contains a `frame_id` that already exists in the inventory?

Treat it as an append-only versioned history (SCD Type 2): close out the existing active record (is_current = false, set valid_to) and insert the incoming CSV row as the new current version so we preserve a full audit trail.

Every upload of an existing `frame_id` will close the current version and insert a new one, even when the values match. A stable frame key will let linked frames keep pointing to the same frame as its versions change.

What should determine when a version takes effect if an incoming row’s `modified_date` is older than the current version’s?
Ignore rows whose modified_date is strictly older than the current active version

PostgreSQL will give each `frame_id` a stable identity and keep its values in version rows, with at most one current version per frame. An incoming row with a strictly older `modified_date` will leave history untouched. A row with an equal or newer timestamp will close the current version and open a new one at the same import time.

# AGENTS.md - Java Spring Boot & gRPC Development Guidelines

Behavioral and architectural guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes while strictly enforcing **SOLID principles**, Spring Boot + gRPC best practices, and clean code standards.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:

* State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
* If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently.
* If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
* If something is unclear (e.g., `.proto` contract changes, transaction boundaries, or domain invariants), stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

* No features or RPC endpoints beyond what was asked.
* No abstractions or Strategy interfaces for single-use code (apply OCP when variation actually exists or is requested).
* No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
* No defensive `try-catch` blocks or error handling for impossible scenarios.
* If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
* Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
* If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it — don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

* Remove imports, variables, fields, or private methods that YOUR changes made unused.
* Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
* "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
* "Refactor X" → "Ensure unit and gRPC integration tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]
[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

## 5. Tech Stack & Conventions

* **Language:** Java 21+ (Prefer `record` for immutable domain DTOs/commands, pattern matching, and modern standard library features).
* **Framework:** Spring Boot 3.4+ with **Spring gRPC** (`org.springframework.grpc:spring-grpc-spring-boot-starter`).
* **Serialization / RPC:** Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) & gRPC.
* **Build Tool:** Maven or Gradle (Respect existing project configuration and `protobuf` compiler plugins).
* **Dependency Injection:** **ALWAYS** use Constructor Injection. Field injection (`@Autowired` on fields) is strictly forbidden.
* **Null Safety:** Avoid returning `null` from methods. Use `Optional<T>` for repository/service lookups that may not yield a result, and use `@NonNull` / `@Nullable` annotations where appropriate.

## 6. Build, Protobuf & Test Commands

Use these standard commands to compile Protobuf definitions and verify changes:

* **Maven:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./mvnw protobuf:compile protobuf:compile-custom`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./mvnw test`
  * Run a single test class: `./mvnw test -Dtest=ClassName`
* **Gradle:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./gradlew generateProto`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./gradlew test`
  * Run a single test class: `./gradlew test --tests "*ClassName"`

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

**These guidelines are working if:** diffs contain fewer unnecessary changes, fewer rewrites occur due to misunderstood requirements, and clarifying questions happen before implementation rather than after mistakes.

5. [ ] Did you avoid speculative abstractions and only touch files directly required by the task?
6. [ ] Are unit tests and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` gRPC stub integration tests included for all new endpoints and business logic?

# Frame inventory schema and version history

**Author** Alex Callow  
**Date** 2026-11-26

## Overview

Use PostgreSQL to store frames and their accepted versions. Each `frame_id` identifies one frame through successive uploads. An incoming row whose `modified_date` is strictly older than the current row is ignored. An equal or newer value closes the previous version and opens the next version at the same import instant.

The supplied extract has 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The migration will create the schema on Spring Boot startup. The exercise calls for a user-driven CSV upload, so the migration will start with empty inventory tables. [CSV](./data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](./INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)

## Analysis

### Raw field mapping

CSV values arrive as text. The types below describe how to parse them for PostgreSQL. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Observed null counts and value sets describe this extract.

| CSV fields | Observed representation | Proposed PostgreSQL mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version` source timestamps, `timestamp without time zone`. |
| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code and counts or distances | `integer` on `frame_version`. The proposed distance unit is metres, consistent with the prototype. |
| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

### Relational boundaries

- `frame_version` has its own primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct `site_no` values map to more than one `inventory_site_no`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

### Version and write rules

| Incoming row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

Use `timestamptz` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, `[valid_from, valid_to)`, with `valid_to` null on a current version. A check constraint ties `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.

## Goals and scope

- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom `/api/health` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Key decisions and implementation staging

The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.

The remaining decision is where to enforce the stale-row and close-and-append operation. A SQL write routine would enforce it as part of this migration and can be tested before an importer exists. A later Spring transaction would keep application write rules with the upload and edit workflows, while this migration would provide the structural constraints and indexes.

# Frame inventory schema and version history

- **Author** Alex Callow
- **Date** 2026-11-26

## Overview

Use PostgreSQL to store frames and their accepted versions. Each `frame_id` identifies one frame through successive uploads. An incoming row whose `modified_date` is strictly older than the current row is ignored. An equal or newer value closes the previous version and opens the next version at the same import instant.

The supplied extract has 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The migration will create the schema on Spring Boot startup. The exercise calls for a user-driven CSV upload, so the migration will start with empty inventory tables. [CSV](./data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](./INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)

## Analysis

### Raw field mapping

CSV values arrive as text. The types below describe how to parse them for PostgreSQL. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Observed null counts and value sets describe this extract.

| CSV fields | Observed representation | Proposed PostgreSQL mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version` source timestamps, `timestamp without time zone`. |
| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code and counts or distances | `integer` on `frame_version`. The proposed distance unit is metres, consistent with the prototype. |
| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

### Relational boundaries

- `frame_version` has its own primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct `site_no` values map to more than one `inventory_site_no`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

### Version and write rules

| Incoming row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

Use `timestamptz` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, `[valid_from, valid_to)`, with `valid_to` null on a current version. A check constraint ties `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.

## Goals and scope

- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom `/api/health` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Key decisions and implementation staging

The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.

The migration owns the schema, keys, validity checks, and indexes. The future
CSV upload, create, and edit paths will call a shared Spring
`@Transactional` service for the stable-row lock and close-and-append
operation. The CSV path supplies `source_modified_at` for the stale check.
Manual edits carry forward the previous source timestamp. Manual creation can
start with null source timestamps.
